kit/sim: server-authoritative fixed-tick simulation

31 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Replication lanes and replayDefining a sim entitySimulation blocks in godot:play/simLane timing, snapshots, and presentationPredicting contested objectsLag compensationScheduling and replaying commandsPredicted spawns — a fired projectileTwo entity kinds, two inputsPromoting a coop gameTuningSimulation constraintsImplementation and test coverage

Use kit/sim for movement, aiming, projectiles, or shared objects whose state must be computed by a trusted authority. Its simulation lane advances gameplay at a fixed tick rate and retains input and state history for prediction and correction. Clients send windows of tick-stamped inputs. The authority computes the accepted state and sends snapshots; each owning client predicts its entities locally and corrects its prediction when a snapshot differs.

Reliable session state such as inventory, score, chat, entity lifetime, and saves remains on kit/session and kit/net.

The package does not import Godot. Its input, snapshot, history, reconciliation, and lag-compensation paths run in headless tests under tests/kitsim.

Replication lanes and replay#

A field tag selects one of three disjoint replication lanes:

tag authority wire applied by
replicate host reliable deltas on arrival
owner owning peer unreliable stream interpolated in the past
predict authority simulation tick-stamped snapshots prediction, reconciliation, and resimulation

Identity, roster, reconnects, spawns, blobs, stats, chat, and reliable commands remain session features. The quickstart introduces the coop model; the sim quickstart shows how to add simulation to that setup. Select the simulation lane per field for fast state such as movement and projectiles that the authority must compute. A field's lane is the tag's first token, so each field uses exactly one lane. Choose either owner or predict; they cannot be combined.

Simulation-lane gameplay runs in a fixed-rate step proc (60 Hz by default). The proc derives predicted fields from their previous values, the current input, and replayable tick data. The authority runs it for final state. The owning client runs it ahead for immediate control response.

When authoritative state for tick T arrives, the client compares it with its recorded prediction. If they differ, the client restores authority at T and replays later ticks from its input history. Bit-exact cross-machine determinism is not required because authority remains final, but replayed code must be stable enough to avoid constant correction.

Step procs may read predicted state, declared inputs, lane_input, and values derived from the tick. They must not read wall clocks, device state, current scene-node transforms, or untracked randomness.

Input packets include a configurable window of recent samples, and newer snapshot batches supersede older ones. If a loss burst exceeds the redundancy window, the authority temporarily holds the player's last accepted input. The client later reconciles to the resulting authority state.

Defining a sim entity#

Tag the entity's simulated fields with predict and mark its tick procedure with @(gd_tick). Script generation discovers the input struct from that procedure's signature. Return values carry tick events to two optional procedures paired by name: <tick>_then handles authority consequences and <tick>_fx handles presentation. The generated thunk, which adapts the typed procedure to the lane's raw-pointer callback, checks which role and simulation pass may call each half.

Here Runner is the game's character type. Its owner field holds the Godot node; the network entity owner is the player whose input drives it.

Odin
Runner :: struct {
	owner:   gd.Node2d,
	net_id:  knet.Net_Id,
	x, y:    f32 `gd:"predict,interp"`,
	vx, vy:  f32 `gd:"predict"`,
	fire_cd: u16 `gd:"predict"`, // cooldown state participates in prediction
	hp:      i32 `gd:"replicate"`, // reliable state updated independently of simulation replay
}

Runner_Input :: struct { // no tag — discovered from the tick proc's signature
	move:    [2]i8,
	buttons: u8,
}

@(gd_tick)
runner_tick :: proc(self: ^Runner, input: Runner_Input) -> (fired: bool) {
	self.vx = f32(input.move[0]) * SPEED // advance using the fixed tick interval
	self.x += self.vx
	if self.fire_cd > 0 {self.fire_cd -= 1}
	if input.buttons & FIRE != 0 && self.fire_cd == 0 {
		self.fire_cd = COOLDOWN
		fired = true // an event trigger, not a verdict — ticks can't reject
	}
	return
}

// Authority only; not called during resimulation.
@(gd_half)
runner_tick_then :: proc(g: ^Game, self: ^Runner, by: knet.Player_Id, fired: bool) {
	if fired { adjudicate_shot(g, self, by) } // lane_rewound lives here
}

// The owning player's live pass only; not called during resimulation.
@(gd_half)
runner_tick_fx :: proc(g: ^Game, self: ^Runner, fired: bool) {
	if fired { muzzle_flash(self) } // local feedback before the authority reply
}

Script generation emits the raw-pointer thunk, role and resimulation checks, runner_sim_set, and recursive input-layout checks. Those checks compare the canonical ABI with the target layout and reject platform-sensitive or padded inputs. Generation also rejects invalid halves and a tick procedure whose entity has no predict fields.

Supported tick signatures are (self), (self, input), (self, lane), and (self, input, lane): a pointer parameter is the lane, and a value parameter is the input. Both halves also accept signatures that omit the game parameter and start with self.

Presenting a tick payload on every screen#

The _fx above runs only for the acting player's live pass. To present the same occurrence on every screen, add mine: bool immediately after self (the parameter name is significant):

Odin
@(gd_half)
runner_tick_fx :: proc(g: ^Game, self: ^Runner, mine: bool, fired: bool) {
	if fired {
		muzzle_flash(self)        // every screen
		if mine {kick_camera(g)}  // feedback for the local player
	}
}
  • The actor presents it immediately with mine = true. Resimulation does not present it again.
  • The authority presents payload events from other actors as they execute, with mine = false.
  • Other clients receive the internal reliable SIM_FACT frame and present it when their watch clock reaches the event's tick. This keeps an effect aligned with the delayed entity that caused it. Occurrences are counted individually, so a batch cannot collapse two occurrences into one.

The actor skips the returned event because its own live pass is expected to have presented it already. Packet loss can break that assumption: the authority may hold the actor's previous input and produce an event that the actor's fresh input did not produce. The actor then misses that effect. Tick payload events are cosmetic one-shots and may be lost this way. If the actor must receive the event even when its input is lost, produce it in an authority world pass (@(gd_step="authority")). Events produced there include the entity owner among their recipients.

Events produced by a world pass#

Use @(gd_event) for a presentation event discovered outside a single entity's tick, such as contact between a player and a ball. An anchor is an entity parameter that selects the event's presentation timeline and owner. When that entity is tracked by the simulation lane, the event uses the lane's watch clock, which follows received state at a delay:

Odin
// The presentation proc you write. `k` is the only entity, so it is the anchor.
@(gd_event = "audience=everyone,timing=auto")
ball_kicked_fx :: proc(g: ^Game, k: ^Kicker, mine: bool, bvx, bvy: f32) {
	kick_sound(bvx, bvy)            // scheduled on the event's display clock
	if mine {kick_camera(g)}        // feedback for the local player
}

// Scriptgen generates this helper. Call it where the sim discovers the event:
if kicked {
	ball_kicked(&g.boot, k, b.roll.vx, b.roll.vy)
}

The generated helper applies the same live-pass, authority, watcher, and resimulation rules as a tick payload event. The anchor's network entity owner determines mine. The anchor names a particular procedure parameter: if a game has hundreds of Enemy instances, anchor=enemy selects the enemy pointer passed to this call.

Select an anchor according to the event's parameters:

  • No entity parameters means a world event. In a lane-owning game, timing=auto selects the watch clock and the authority is its local producer.
  • One entity parameter is the inferred anchor.
  • With two or more entity parameters, name one parameter explicitly, such as @(gd_event="anchor=target,timing=auto").
  • Use anchor=none only when the authority/world clock is intentional despite carrying entity references.

Put all typed entity parameters between the game and mine. They must be lane-tracked script classes. The anchor travels in the internal event header; every other entity reference travels as a Net_Id and is resolved to that peer's local pointer before presentation. Arguments after mine must be wire primitives. Scriptgen rejects ambiguous anchors, names that are not entity parameters, and untracked entity types at build time.

Announce an anchored event before untracking or despawning its anchor. The generated helper rejects events whose anchor no longer exists, so no peer presents them. A predicted event that the authority never confirms may still appear locally. Speedball's kick is the worked example. Declare presentation events for either session or simulation clocks with @(gd_event) and call them through the generated helper that accepts ^Boot.

For a local diagnostic such as a debug print in a tick body, gate on ksim.lane_live(&lane) to skip resimulation. Do not read lane.resimming directly.

For a mine-form tick event, at least one returned value must be bool; the half runs on ticks where any boolean payload is true. All returned payloads must be wire primitives. Scriptgen reports either violation at build time. Use a plain owner-only _fx (without mine) for continuous local presentation such as an engine hum, or for an effect that should not appear on every screen.

The game declares input sampling and world passes with typed procedures and attributes too. @(gd_sample) marks the procedure that reads hardware; it is never called during resimulation. Scriptgen checks its input struct against the tick's input type at build time and rejects a mismatch.

Declare field-level input validation on the input struct:

Odin
Move_Mode :: enum u8 {On_Foot, Driving}

@(gd_input)
Runner_Input :: struct {
	aim:     [2]f32 `gd:"unit"`,
	trigger: f32    `gd:"finite,range=0:1"`,
	move:    [2]i8  `gd:"range=-1:1"`,
	mode:    Move_Mode `gd:"enum"`,
	buttons: u8     `gd:"mask=0x07"`,
}

range clamps each scalar/array component. unit rejects non-finite vector components and scales only magnitudes above one, preserving analog strength. finite, enum, and mask reject values that have no legal authored meaning. The generated sanitizer runs after local sampling and transactionally over every received window before any authority buffer changes.

Each received input window must fit its size and redundancy limits. Across windows, a seat may send at most 16 input classes in a 32 KiB SIM_INPUT payload. Generated and hand-built lanes assert these aggregate limits at registration. The authority rejects an oversized packet before creating per-class buffers.

For cross-field or game-state rules, add @(gd_sample="validate") and the typed <sample>_validate(self, input) -> bool hook (or name one with validate=PROC). It runs after the generated field rules; returning false rejects the complete multi-class packet. @(gd_step) is the world pass, run after entity ticks. A game may declare one of each kind: a bare @(gd_step) runs on every peer, including resimulation, while @(gd_step="authority") runs once per real tick on the authority. Keep the two procedures separate so the generator can apply the execution policy:

Odin
@(gd_sample = "validate")
game_sample :: proc(self: ^Game, tick: u64, input: ^Runner_Input) {
	input.move = quantize_axes()
	input.buttons = read_buttons()
}

game_sample_validate :: proc(self: ^Game, input: ^Runner_Input) -> bool {
	// Field ranges/masks are already canonical here. Keep only relationships
	// that cannot be expressed one field at a time.
	return input.trigger == 0 || input.buttons & BTN_FIRE != 0
}

@(gd_step) // everywhere, live + resim: contact for the pairs this peer simulates
game_contact :: proc(self: ^Game, tick: u64) {
	resolve_overlaps(self)
}

@(gd_step = "authority") // host alone: adjudication, respawns, the match clock
game_step :: proc(self: ^Game, tick: u64) {
	run_respawns(self, tick)
}

(The tick: u64 param is optional in both slots; a pass that doesn't read the clock declares proc(self: ^Game).)

Using an authority step without a simulation lane#

A package with no @(gd_tick) classes has no simulation lane. In that case, @(gd_step = "authority") uses the boot accumulator: scriptgen generates <snake>_step(self, ticks) with the authority check, fixed-step loop, and same-frame edge pass, called from <game>_net_frame. Cavecrawl's cave_host_tick demonstrates this setup. The coop loop has no absolute tick, so declare proc(self) and count ticks in a gd:"backup" field if needed. Adding a simulation lane changes the generated routing without changing the attribute.

For a game root with one Boot, Session, Comms, and Lane field, the generated game-network facade connects these components. Pass a named network profile when attaching, then override lane settings when measurements call for it:

Odin
// ready(): Boot + entities + lane in one generated call
cfg := kboot.network_profile(.Listen_Server_Action)
cfg.lane.smooth_cut = 48
game_net_attach(self, kboot.Options{/* ... */}, cfg)

The generated <class>_lane_init supplies the input size, typed procedures, and world-pass callbacks; boot_lane connects the lane to Boot. Both are public for custom game roots. The generated entity table includes each ticking class's Sim_Set, allowing the factory to track and untrack its entities on the lane. <game>_net_frame calls boot_pump, which runs lane_frame and lane_present every frame and forwards Ev_Owner_Changed.

Entity thunks run in track order on every simulated tick, including replay, using each entity owner's input. A nil input leaves the entity coasting; this applies to inputless types and to remote entities whose state a client receives from the authority. After entity ticks, the optional everywhere world pass handles replayable cross-entity work such as contact. The authority world pass handles accepted world outcomes such as respawns and wave scheduling.

An input class groups entities by the distinct input struct in their @(gd_tick) signatures. lane_init registers the primary class (class 0), and lane_add_input_class registers each additional class. Each packet carries one window per class; see Two entity kinds, two inputs. Two entities of the same kind driven by one player share a window, so compose their intent into one struct.

Inputs cross the wire as a memory copy of the struct, with no per-field wire encoding. To quantize an input, declare its quantized type. Quickdraw's aim uses a u16 turn fraction with ~0.005° resolution, encoded when sampling and decoded in the tick. A world pass that reads inputs uses the typed view:

Odin
input, drives := ksim.lane_input_of(&g.lane, owner, Kicker_Input)
if !drives {continue} // a pair this peer doesn't simulate

Tests and games without generated code can call the same procedures directly: lane_init, lane_set_sim with a rawptr sample callback and two Step_Procs (everywhere, then authority), lane_track / lane_track_set, and explicit lane_frame/lane_present calls. In this setup, lane_present is optional. Until its first call, the presented latch allows received snapshots to update watched fields directly. After that call, presentation updates those fields. A client that omits lane_present therefore continues to show received state.

Reinitializing a session does not reset lane state. The app route survives, but the tick anchor and state ledgers remain tied to the previous authority. Call lane_destroy then lane_init to reset them. Destruction zeroes the lane; calling lane_init on a live lane asserts.

Simulation blocks in godot:play/sim#

Embed a godot:play/sim block to add reusable simulated behavior to an entity. Scriptgen includes the block's gd:"predict" fields in the entity's replication descriptor and calls the block's @(gd_tick) after the entity's own tick. The entity can therefore write movement intent before the block integrates it. The import alias is psim:

Odin
import psim "godot:play/sim"

Kicker :: struct {
	...
	run:  psim.Mover, // momentum movement: the tick writes run.tx/ty, the block integrates
	kick: psim.Cool,  // predicted cooldown: psim.ready(&k.kick, KICK_CD) gates and re-arms
}
  • psim.Cool implements a predicted cooldown with due / arm / ready, the same operations as play.Pace. Pace stores a deadline against a clock supplied by the caller; it is host-local state and is never sent. Cool counts down within the simulation, so the client can predict a revolver's firing cadence or a kick's recovery and reproduce it during replay.
  • psim.Mover implements momentum-based 2D movement. The entity's tick writes its target velocity, and the block approaches that velocity. Set accel = 1 to reach it immediately. Configuration such as acceleration and bounds uses plain, untagged fields. Set it at spawn on every peer; it is not replicated.
  • psim.Roller integrates a shared rolling body's motion with friction, a hard speed ceiling, and wall bounces that reduce speed. The game implements gameplay outcomes. Speedball detects goals from the roller's position clamp: a crossing places the ball exactly on the line for one tick, allowing the ball's tick to detect the goal and predict its reset.

Driving a block yourself: gd:"manual". By default, a block's tick runs after its containing entity's tick. Call it manually when the entity must use the integrated result immediately, such as resolving a crate overlap after movement, or must skip integration, such as freezing a dead avatar's cooldown. Tag the embedded field gd:"manual" to suppress the generated tick call, then call the block's tick at the required point:

Odin
fire: psim.Cool `gd:"manual"`, // tick explicitly in the parent procedure

@(gd_tick)
gunner_tick :: proc(self: ^Gunner, in: Gunner_Input) -> (fired: bool) {
	if self.hp <= 0 {return} // leave the cooldown unchanged while dead
	if in.buttons & FIRE != 0 && psim.ready(&self.fire, FIRE_CD) {fired = true}
	psim.cool_tick(&self.fire) // driven here, on the alive path
}

The block's predicted fields remain in the descriptor and on the wire; manual suppresses only the generated call. The entity can call the block conditionally, change its ordering, or skip it. An untagged embedded field retains the default ordering. Quickdraw's revolver freezes its cooldown while dead by skipping that call.

Scriptgen checks blocks in the SDK's two packages. A block in godot:play with predicted fields produces an error directing it to play/sim; a play/sim block with no predicted fields produces the reverse error. These checks do not restrict game-local blocks. They ensure that SDK blocks imported with the psim. prefix contain state that participates in resimulation.

Lane timing, snapshots, and presentation#

  • Anchoring. A client waits to tick or send input until its first snapshot batch establishes the server's tick. It adopts that state and starts a couple of ticks ahead. Afterward, a ±2% timescale adjustment grows or shrinks the lead toward the target input headroom, using the batch header's input-ack echo. This needs no separate clock synchronization or tick jumps.
  • Snapshots use an acknowledged baseline. The server computes deltas for each entity's predicted fields against the newest batch the client confirmed applying in full. A client acknowledges a batch only after every row applies. An unknown entity id, such as a spawn still in transit, is skipped by row length and prevents the acknowledgement from advancing. A missing baseline causes a per-entity full row, without a keyframe-request message.
  • Predict-self. The client records its own entities in state-history ledgers and reconciles them. It watches other entities: received state updates them, and lane_present renders them on a delayed watch clock by blending between batches per field. This uses Lerp_Kind, as streams do, with the same clamp-and-hold rule: it never extrapolates.
  • Correction smoothing. Reconciliation immediately sets simulation state to authority state and records it in the ledger. For float interp fields, lane_present adds a decaying render error with a 63 ms half-life, the same constant used by the puppet. This smooths the displayed correction. If the error exceeds a nonzero smooth_cut, it is cleared and the corrected pose appears immediately. Fields contain simulation values during lane_frame and presentation values after lane_present. Before ticking again, the lane restores simulation values from the ledger, so the game can continue copying fields to nodes after presentation.
  • Game callbacks run in the frame call. Packet handlers store received bytes. The lane calls game code from lane_frame on the caller's stack.
  • Possession. Forward the session's Ev_Owner_Changed to lane_set_owner(l, id, player) on every peer. The authority changes which player's input buffer drives the entity and which player's rewound queries exclude it. A client changes the entity between predicted and watched state, seeding a new prediction ledger from the freshest received state.

Predicting contested objects#

With predict-self, a client watches shared fast objects such as a ball, crown, or flag. They render in the past, and a local interaction waits for the round trip to the authority. Mark an entity @(gd_tick = "contested") to have every peer predict it. Local contact can then take effect on the client's predicted timeline. The server still decides the accepted state. If an opponent touched the object first on the server, the client reconciles its prediction and smooths the displayed correction.

Contested prediction adds resimulation work on every peer and can produce corrections when peers disagree about contact. Keep authority consequences in _then so replay cannot apply them twice. Put predicted resets in the tick itself: Speedball's ball detects a goal and handles the kickoff freeze in its own tick, allowing each screen to reset the ball as soon as its simulation crosses the line. The authority updates the score. Handle contact in the world pass only for pairs whose inputs this peer has: the local player's pairs on a client and every player's pairs on the server. A remote touch then arrives as an authority result.

Constraints for contested prediction:

  • Contested entities must simulate their own motion. A ball can integrate velocity between snapshots on every peer. An input-driven avatar without remote input would instead remain stationary on a client and repeatedly require correction.
  • Presentation follows a claim. A claim selects the displayed pose; it does not grant authority over gameplay. Call lane_claim(l, id) each tick that local simulation influences the contested entity, such as during contact in the world pass. The entity then displays its predicted pose. Without a claim, it displays the watched pose, aligning a remote touch with the delayed avatar that caused it. Otherwise the screen would show a predicted ball reacting before the remote avatar reached it. Claim weight rises immediately and decays over ~a quarter second. This is the continuous form of net.md's test for whether local simulation caused the change.
  • Predict-world also predicts remote avatars. Enable Lane_Config.echo_inputs and mark the avatars contested too. Batches echo every player's held input, allowing every peer to tick every entity and extrapolate remote inputs from the held values. Speedball uses this model. The scene shares one predicted timeline, and contested entities display their predicted poses without claims. Remote contacts appear beside the avatars making them immediately. Held inputs often differ from the next received inputs, so this model adds resimulation on nearly every batch, frequent small smoothed corrections on remote avatars, and a few echo bytes per player per batch. Choose it for contact-driven games. Predict-self with lag compensation suits games that need accurate rendered targets: Quickdraw watches targets without extrapolating them. The remaining claim rules apply when clients predict only the shared object.
  • Keep a claim while its cause persists. After a kick, continue claiming while the ball moves quickly because of that touch. Release when it slows, when the predicted and watched timelines nearly coincide, or when an opponent contests it. Releasing merely because the ball is far away blends toward the watched pose, which trails a fast ball by speed × timeline skew. That blend can pull the ball backward during its flight. The sp_step claim block in examples/claimball demonstrates holding while fast and releasing when slow.

Compare the three soccer examples when choosing a model: examples/slopball uses coop peer authority, examples/speedball uses predict-world with echoed avatar inputs and no claims, and examples/claimball uses predict-self with presentation claims on the contested ball. In claimball, every screen predicts the ball; a local claim selects its predicted pose for display. The onboarding's competitive turn compares the same three models.

Lag compensation#

Odin
// Judge the shooter's hitscan on the authority, in _then or a world pass.
judged_at := ksim.lane_rewound_begin(&g.lane, shooter)
g.hit = trace_shot(g) // Other entities use the shooter’s historical view;
                      // the shooter’s own state remains live.
ksim.lane_rewound_end(&g.lane)

Write the hit test between the begin and end calls. This avoids passing a context struct through a rawptr callback. The calls must not nest, and no code may track or untrack entities between them. For tests or table-driven weapons, lane_rewound(l, shooter, user, query) provides the same query through a callback.

Rewind changes only the predicted fields of tracked entities other than the shooter's own. Delta-lane fields such as hp, scores, and gear, untracked entities, and game-side maps retain their current values. Quickdraw tests a rewound pose but applies damage to current hp, so a player already dead cannot absorb a new bullet. If a hit predicate needs the target's shield state at the time the shooter saw it, that state must be in the predicted fields too. Otherwise the predicate combines a past pose with the current shield state.

Each input packet carries the sender's snapshot acknowledgement and render offset; the input buffer records both alongside each input. Before judging a shot, the server verifies that its acknowledgement names a recent batch issued to that seat and has not regressed. The client still only claims to have applied the batch: a valid replication baseline does not prove what it displayed.

The authority limits credible acknowledgement age to ceil((observed RTT + 2·jitter) / tick_dt) + margin + snap_every and limits the reported render offset to its configured watch_delay + snap_every. The extra snapshot cadence allows normal interpolation around the watch target without accepting a client-reported stall. The sum, capped again by rewind_max, is the seat's current competitive rewind envelope: the maximum credible rewind age in ticks. lane_rewind_envelope(l, shooter) exposes it. Until the authority has a pong sample for the seat, this limit is zero and queries use current state.

Within that limit, rewind uses predict_blend over the state ledger to reconstruct the pair of snapshots the shooter reports blending. Using the freshest acknowledgement instead would advance the view by the client's lead plus transit time between sampling and adjudication. Using a single tick would lose the interpolation needed for near-tangent shots. Quickdraw's duel acceptance test measures this behavior: most aimable shots land at 240 ms RTT.

rewind_max (default ~250 ms) remains the absolute limit on how far the server favors the shooter's past view. An older issued acknowledgement, a reported render-clock stall, or an inflated field cannot grant the full window; the measured connection and configured limits bound the reconstructed view. Rewind can still let a shot hit someone just after they reach cover. A snapshot acknowledgement cannot prove which frame the player actually saw, so the render offset remains a bounded hint.

Scheduling and replaying commands#

A Kit command requests a discrete action with arguments. Its predicate may reject the request; an accepted request executes once. On a ticking class, @(gd_command) uses the same declaration as the coop model: validate and mutate the target, then handle accepted authority consequences in the paired _then procedure. The simulation lane schedules the command within its tick pipeline:

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED)
gunner_buy :: proc(self: ^Gunner, item: u8) -> bool {
	if self.gold < price_of(item) {return false}
	self.gold -= price_of(item) // delta lane: reverted on rejection
	self.gear = item            // predicted: replayed by every resim
	return true
}

// Issue through the Boot wrapper from an input handler or bot.
// The wrapper returns the same knet.Action_Outcome type as a cooperative command.
outcome := gunner_buy_cmd(&g.boot, g.me_gun, ITEM_BOOTS)
if outcome.reason == .Rate {show_slow_down_feedback()}

The generated wrapper schedules the command at the client's next tick and sends it reliably with that tick stamp. The client's simulation lead gives it time to arrive before the server reaches the tick. If it arrives late, the server executes it at its next tick without rewriting history.

The client executes the command once at its scheduled tick. Resimulation reapplies its recorded predicted-field writes, avoiding a second predicate check against gold the command already spent. On the server, commands run after entity thunks and before the world pass. A rejection immediately unwinds the speculative delta-lane writes; the next reconciliation removes speculative predicted-field changes and smooths the displayed correction.

Every verb declares the same typed policy as the co-op lane. Bare @(gd_command) is owner-only and non-predicted; knet.ACTION_OWNER_PREDICTED opts into owner speculation, knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT opens a world interaction, and knet.ACTION_AUTHORITY never crosses client ingress. Prediction requires both an optimistic action policy and a prediction ledger: marking an entity contested does not silently predict every verb, and choosing a predicted policy does not make a watched entity predictable. Two commands scheduled for the same tick run in execution order; each predicate decides whether its request still applies, as when two players try to spike the same ball. Commands queue per entity. A rejection unwinds delta-lane speculation in order while preserving the effects of surviving commands. The wrapper returns the same Action_Outcome as co-op: .state says whether the request was scheduled, .reason names a local access/rate/malformed/stale refusal, .seq correlates the final callback, and .model is .Scheduled.

The authority verdict reaches the ordinary generated session callbacks. A client's <game>_command_rejected half receives the addressed command and an Action_Reject_Reason; the host's <game>_command_executed half receives the same reason for diagnostics. Predicate failure and timeout are therefore distinct without a lane-specific event API. Scheduled timeouts use an independent lane-frame clock, so authority loss still expires actions when the simulation clock itself has stopped waiting for snapshots.

If the predicate needs the issuer's identity, declare by: knet.Player_Id immediately after the receiver. During client speculation, the lane supplies the local seat; on the authority it supplies the recorded issuer, the same value passed to _then. This value is never sent as a command argument, so a client cannot choose another issuer when interacting with a contested entity. The name is reserved: a wire argument called by is a build error.

Replay normally reapplies a command's recorded bytes, so prefer absolute mutations such as gear = item. For relative effects such as an impulse or knockback, declare <verb>_apply(self, <wire args>) to implement the predicted-field mutation. Resimulation reruns this _apply half with the recorded arguments against corrected state. An additive impulse then applies to the corrected velocity rather than restoring the old resulting velocity. When an _apply half exists, the main command must not write predicted fields; its predicate and delta-lane writes still execute once.

Odin
@(gd_command = knet.ACTION_ANY_SEAT_PREDICTED)
ball_spike :: proc(self: ^Ball, px, py: f32) -> bool {
	return self.hold == 0 && in_reach(self, px, py) // verdict + (any) delta writes
}
@(gd_half)
ball_spike_apply :: proc(self: ^Ball, px, py: f32) {
	self.vx += ... // relative mutation, recomputed on each resimulation
}

Predicted spawns — a fired projectile#

To show a projectile immediately when the player fires, create a local predicted entity before the authority's spawn arrives. It simulates its flight locally and records history for correction. When the authority announces the projectile, the factory assigns its authoritative id to the existing local entity instead of creating a second bullet.

Declare the projectile as an inputless @(gd_tick) entity that integrates its own motion, with an entity=Bullet:id scene. The authority spawns it in the firing tick's _then half. The _fx half creates the local prediction only when mine is true and this peer is not the authority. This check prevents a hosting player, whose _then already created the bullet, from spawning it twice. Both halves call the same helper:

Odin
@(gd_tick) // the flight: pure predicted state, `landed` routes to the splash
bullet_tick :: proc(self: ^Bullet) -> (landed: bool) { ...self.x += self.vx... }

@(gd_half)
gunner_tick_then :: proc(g: ^Game, self: ^Gunner, by: knet.Player_Id, lobbed: bool) {
	if lobbed { lob_bullet(g, self, by) } // AUTHORITY: the real spawn
}
@(gd_half)
gunner_tick_fx :: proc(g: ^Game, self: ^Gunner, mine: bool, lobbed: bool) {
	// The hosting player's authority callback already spawned the bullet.
	// Predict a local bullet only on a non-authority owner client.
	if lobbed && mine && !ksim.lane_is_authority(&g.lane) {
		lob_bullet(g, self, g.ses.me)
	}
}

lob_bullet :: proc(g: ^Game, gun: ^Gunner, owner: knet.Player_Id) {
	b, bid := bullet_spawn(&g.boot, owner) // allocate through the shared authority/prediction helper
	b.x, b.y, b.vx, b.vy, b.life = ... // the muzzle and the arc
	kboot.boot_spawn_send(&g.boot, bid) // host announces; client no-ops
}

Scriptgen generates bullet_spawn for the entity= declaration. For a ticking entity it calls kboot.boot_fire_spawn, which creates an authoritative network id through session_spawn_make on the authority and a local predicted node under a provisional id on the client.

Born-tick gating prevents a correction for a tick before the local spawn from restarting its flight from stale state. Such corrections can arrive throughout the first round trip while the server runs behind the client's prediction. When the authority's Ev_Spawned arrives, the factory matches it to the local projectile and replaces its provisional id. The node and flight ledger remain intact for later reconciliation. If the authority refuses the fire or never spawns the projectile, the local prediction is culled and its node freed. Splash damage is judged against current server state without rewind, because a slow projectile is intended to be dodged.

The right-click lob in examples/quickdraw demonstrates this behavior. Its native acceptance test creates the predicted bullet on the client's own tick without waiting for a round trip.

Two entity kinds, two inputs#

One player can drive two entity kinds on the same tick, such as an avatar and a vehicle or a duelist and a companion drone. Each kind declares its own @(gd_tick) input struct, forming a separate input class. The client samples each class once per tick and sends one window per class in a single upstream packet. The host buffers each player's classes separately to absorb arrival jitter. Each entity tick reads its own class, and reconciliation of one entity leaves the other entity's state intact.

Declare a second @(gd_sample), one per input type:

Odin
// two ticking kinds, two input structs
@(gd_tick) gunner_tick :: proc(self: ^Gunner, in: Gunner_Input) { ... }
@(gd_tick) drone_tick  :: proc(self: ^Drone,  in: Drone_Input)  { ... }

// two device reads on the game root — scriptgen matches each to its class by
// the struct it writes (one sample per input type; a second on the same type
// is a build error)
@(gd_sample) qd_sample    :: proc(self: ^Game, tick: u64, in: ^Gunner_Input) { ... }
@(gd_sample) drone_sample :: proc(self: ^Game, tick: u64, in: ^Drone_Input)  { ... }

Scriptgen assigns each distinct input type a stable wire id, sorted by name with the primary class at 0. It records the class in each Sim_Set and registers all classes in <game>_lane_init: lane_init registers the primary and lane_add_input_class registers the rest. Track entities with their generated Sim_Set to route input during live simulation, prediction, and resimulation. A single-input game registers one class and retains the same single-class wire representation.

A Lane keeps one history ring per class the local seat drives; the host keeps one buffer per (player, class). A batch acknowledges the oldest of the newest input ticks across a player's classes. This lets the client maintain enough lead for the class furthest behind and trim every ring to that common floor. The limit is one driven entity per class per player. Two same-kind entities driven by one player share a window; use distinct input structs or combine their intent in one struct.

Quickdraw's companion drone in examples/quickdraw demonstrates multiple classes. Its native acceptance test predicts the drone on the client's own tick while steering it in a different direction from the gunner, verifying independent input routing from one seat.

Promoting a coop game#

Because the lane is selected per field, a session-replication game can migrate one contested entity at a time. The worked comparison is examples/slopball → examples/speedball:

  1. Keep session features in place. Identity, roster, chat, stats, spawns, saves, generated helpers, and the entity factory support both models. Chests, inventories, and scores stay on the delta lane with their commands.
  2. Retag the contested fast state. owner (movement the peer owned) becomes predict: the field's writer changes from "its owner's stream" to "the server's simulation, predicted locally". Keep interp on displayed floats.
  3. Move its writes into a @(gd_tick). Frame-rate mutation becomes a fixed-rate pure step: (predicted fields, input) → predicted fields. This is the main simulation rewrite, and it is where engine physics must become query-based kinematics (slopball's play.Puppet ball becomes speedball's forty lines of bounce arithmetic; see Simulation constraints).
  4. Declare and sample the input struct. Mark it @(gd_input), put field ranges/finite/unit/enum/mask rules beside the fields, and sample it in @(gd_sample), the one place that still touches hardware.
  5. Add only game predicates by hand. Use @(gd_sample = "validate") for cross-field or game-state invariants; the generated field sanitizer already runs locally and at authority admission.
  6. Sort the consequences. Cross-entity outcomes move to <tick>_then (authority), local presentation to <tick>_fx (live pass). Discrete verbs on delta-lane state keep their @(gd_command)s.
  7. Remove obsolete ownership arbitration. Logic that chose which peer simulates owner-streamed state may no longer apply after the authority takes over. Keep presentation claims where local contact needs an immediate displayed response.
  8. Attach the network components: let <game>_net_attach(self, options, cfg) validate a named network profile, install the generated lane, and migrate entities one at a time. A hybrid game is a supported end state. A custom shell can call <game>_lane_init + boot_lane directly. Command and spawn call sites continue using <verb>_cmd(&boot, …) and <entity>_spawn(&boot, …) in both models; the generated bodies choose the appropriate execution path.

After promotion, the authority derives the selected fields from admitted input instead of accepting client-written positions. This adds fixed-tick authoring, history, and server simulation cost. It also enables authoritative rewind queries. Input validation and a trusted authority remain necessary; the field tag alone is not a complete security policy. See Timelines for model selection.

Tuning#

Lane_Config (zero = the default): hz 60 · snap_every 3 (20 Hz batches) · margin 2 (target input headroom, ticks) · slots 128 (ledger depth) · redundancy 8 · rewind_max hz/4 · lead_max max(margin + rewind_max + 2×snap_every, slots/2, 8) (the furthest client-stamped input/verb tick accepted ahead of authority time) · watch_delay 2×snap_every · smooth_halflife 0.063 s · smooth_cut 0 (never cut; set it in world units for teleport-heavy games) · tolerance 0 (exact reconcile; set it in world units to leave smaller continuous held-input drift uncorrected in predict-world) · snapshot_budget 0 (unlimited at the low-level; named profiles install a measured per-recipient ceiling).

lane_init validates the configuration as one set: negative values are invalid; cadence, margin, rewind, lead, and watch delay must fit the ring; redundancy cannot exceed the receiver cap; and watch_delay cannot exceed 31 (the render offset rides the wire in eighths of a tick, in one byte). echo_inputs with tolerance 0 warns once, since that pairing resims on nearly every batch; set the tolerance in world units. For a netgraph, use lane.stat_reconciles and lane.stat_resims to show corrections and bursts of replay work. Host-side counters for version skew and invalid traffic include stat_input_drops (input windows dropped for an unknown class id), stat_input_rejected (malformed or future windows), stat_ack_rejected (unissued, regressing, misaligned, or stale snapshot claims), stat_cmd_capped (verbs refused by the per-player cap), stat_cmd_rate_dropped (verbs refused by the shared action token bucket), stat_cmd_rejected (replay/bounds/access refusals), and stat_echo_dropped (predict-world rows past the u8 batch ceiling). Snapshot telemetry is stat_snap_full, stat_snap_delta, stat_snap_suppressed, stat_snap_deferred, stat_snap_aoi_culled, and stat_snap_bytes. lane_net_stats collects these with input gaps, ack age, current command queue, rewind depth, resimulated ticks, and measured replay seconds. Games using Boot can read the installed lane's statistics through kboot.boot_net_stats.

Snapshot AOI, budgets, and sparse recovery#

Simulation snapshots reuse session_set_interest and session_set_focus to select an area of interest (AOI) for each recipient. An entity owned by the recipient is always eligible; other predicted entities must be in that recipient's session AOI. When snapshot_budget is nonzero, the authority sends owned entities first, then the stalest eligible rows, with distance as the tie-break. Work that does not fit is deferred rather than growing the packet.

Unchanged entities emit no row. The authority records that their acknowledged value was represented at the new batch tick, and the receiver carries the same value into its baseline history. AOI-culled and budget-deferred entities are not marked represented. If one later re-enters after the global acknowledgement advanced, its first row is full, so a global batch ack can never authorize a delta against state that recipient did not receive. This is why sparse batches do not need a keyframe-request protocol.

For lag compensation, monitor stat_rewind_clamped. It counts rewound queries limited by the authority's measured-connection bounds, configured render-hint cap, or absolute rewind_max. A clamp or two before timing measurements settle is normal. A persistently increasing count can mean that the client reports an older view than its measured connection and lane settings allow, its simulation lead needs adjustment, or the configured ceiling is too small for the link. Quickdraw's duel acceptance test checks this counter because a hit count alone does not reveal shots consistently judged at the permitted rewind limit.

Per-field reconciliation and smoothing. Float fields can override lane defaults through their tags, allowing a fast contested object and a precise avatar to use different correction behavior within the same lane:

  • slack=N (world units) overrides tolerance: the allowed drift before reconciliation. This applies only to floats. Discrete predicted state always reconciles exactly when any byte differs.
  • glide=N (seconds) overrides smooth_halflife: the half-life of the displayed correction error. A larger value makes the displayed correction more gradual.
  • cut=N (world units) overrides smooth_cut: the error beyond which correction immediately snaps the displayed pose. If any field exceeds its own cut, the whole pose snaps together.

glide=/cut= require a predict,interp float field because they control render error; a predicted field without interpolation snaps on reconciliation. slack= requires a predict float. Scriptgen reports an error if a tag is used on an incompatible field.

Simulation constraints#

  • Step procedures rerun. Anything a step reads must be recorded in history or derived from the tick. Reading knet.now_s() introduces a value that changes during replay and can cause misprediction. Sample devices only in game_sample.
  • Mutate predicted fields within the tick pipeline. A client write outside that pipeline is absent from replay history and will be erased by the next reconciliation. Use @(gd_command) for discrete mutations; on a ticking class, these commands are scheduled and replayed within the pipeline. See "Scheduling and replaying commands".
  • Engine physics cannot be replayed. Predicted movement must use query-based kinematics. A rigid body can use the simulation lane only if its step procedure implements integration. Engine ray and shape casts are replayable only against static geometry such as walls or the arena. During replay, the physics server still holds current node poses. A cast against another moving entity's collider would therefore query the latest frame rather than the replayed tick. Test entity-to-entity contact in Odin using the tracked structs' fields, as the examples' overlap checks do.
  • Delta-lane reads can cause corrections when the value changes. A tick may read delta-lane fields, but replay sees their current values and clients receive their changes after network transit. Around a death, Quickdraw's if self.hp <= 0 gate lets the client predict a step the server refuses; presentation smoothing reduces the visible correction. This may be acceptable for rare changes. Mirror frequently changing state into a predicted field when it must replay with the tick.
  • Watched entities render in the past. Their watch_delay works like the delay on owner streams. Account for the difference between their displayed time and the local avatar's predicted time when handling interactions.
  • Present before updating nodes. lane_present writes displayed values into fields: interpolation for watched entities and smoothed corrections for predicted entities. Code that needs simulation state must run inside tick procedures or the Step_Proc, before lane_present. The ledger retains simulation state for access outside that pipeline.

Implementation and test coverage#

The repository currently implements the input pipeline, ledgers, snapshots, reconciliation, lane driver, lag compensation, watched interpolation, render-error smoothing, possession, predicted spawns, tick payloads and world events, multiple input classes, generated authoring, and the play/sim blocks.

tests/kitsim covers convergence under loss and blackout, input-class routing, glide versus snap behavior, and event timing. tests/repgen covers generated contracts. Quickdraw and Speedball add multi-process acceptance tests for the main competitive paths.

Implemented limits include declarative input constraints, shared traffic budgets and authority admission checks, protocol-wide payload ceilings, per-recipient snapshot budgets, AOI, and sparse snapshots that preserve acknowledgement safety. Decoder and property-test corpora check protocol handling. These mechanisms do not establish support for arbitrary scale. Simulation event tuples are capped at 4 KiB, command arguments at the action-policy bound, input packets at 32 KiB, and every simulation message remains inside the session's 256 KiB app-message / 1 MiB packet envelope. The benchmark-backed supported starting points are published by network_profile_envelope and documented in profiles; measure your game logic and engine work before raising them.

See net for the wire format, descriptors, blend math, and tick support used by this lane; session for identity and reliable state; and play for coop components, including Puppet for engine-driven physics and play/sim for replayable integration.
